item.title: The More You Notice, the More Choices You Have
item.description:
Attention

The More You Notice, the More Choices You Have

What we notice shapes both how we understand a situation and the options we see.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Better attention helps us notice relevant information before assumptions narrow what we think is possible.
  • Attention requires both focus and openness to information we may not expect or want to find.
  • We can improve our attention through practice, helping us notice more and choose more intentionally.

When you see or hear something, are you doing anything, or are you simply waiting for the world to hit your senses?

Most of us think seeing happens when we open our eyes and hearing happens when sounds reach our ears. Our senses receive information, our brains process it, and then we decide what to do.

Yet seeing something passively is not the same as actively noticing it.

We can learn to pay attention in ways that affect not only what but also how much we notice. The goal is not to take in everything. The goal is to keep ourselves from narrowing our scope before we have noticed enough to judge well and to become better at recognizing what is worth noticing.

Otherwise, we may miss things standing right in front of us. For example, in Simons’s and Chabris’s famous “gorilla” experiments, participants focusing on counting basketball passes sometimes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. Their eyes were working perfectly well, but they could only see what they were looking for.

The Benefits of Paying Better Attention

Better attention improves judgment because it shapes what information becomes available for us to consider. Think about the last difficult conversation you had. I am sure you heard what the other person was saying, but did you notice their tone or their facial expressions? Recent experimental research has reinforced the importance of looking beyond words. When facial, vocal, and verbal emotional cues were systematically varied, facial and vocal cues more strongly shaped how emotional meaning was perceived than verbal cues. That is one reason why meaning and intent can be harder to communicate over text, since many interpretive cues are missing.

Paying attention also means noticing yourself. A tightening chest, clenched jaw, quickened breath, or impulse to interrupt is also information that something inside us might be influencing what we are seeing or hearing.

We Never Notice Everything but We Could Notice More

Attention is necessarily selective. Far more is happening around us and inside us than we can consciously process. We have to focus on some things and filter out others. Still, we can become better at directing attention, sustaining it, and widening or shifting attention when the situation requires it.

Simone Weil described attention as a “negative effort,” by which she meant suspending our thoughts long enough to become receptive to what is occurring around us. This kind of receptivity is not passive. It takes discipline to resist being pulled toward whatever is loudest, most urgent, or most familiar. It also takes discipline to remove ourselves from the center of focus.

How Attention Shapes Meaning & Options

Imagine that you are speaking to someone who gives you a half-smile. How quickly might you interpret that half-smile as evidence that the person thinks what you are saying is ridiculous? Yet half-smiles are ambiguous. There are other ways to “see” them. The person might not be mocking you. They might have remembered something funny or are uncomfortable. Their half-smile may have nothing to do with you at all.

The distinction matters because each interpretation makes different responses seem reasonable. If I am certain you are mocking me, I may become defensive. If I recognize that I saw a half-smile but do not yet know what it means, I can wait for more information or ask a question.

That is why attention is the starting point for good judgment. More skillfully directed attention expands what we notice while helping us determine what information is relevant. Better information can reveal more plausible interpretations. More plausible interpretations can help generate more viable options. None of this guarantees better action, but it gives us a better chance of choosing wisely rather than merely reacting.

The encouraging part is that we can learn to pay attention better.

Practice Doesn’t Make Perfect, It Makes Room

One practice I use with students to improve attention comes from Visual Thinking Strategies, originally developed for visual literacy and art education. Looking at a work of art, students are asked three questions: What is going on in this picture? What do you see that makes you say that? What more can you find?

Students ground what they think is happening in what they can see, yet they are also challenged not to take their seeing for granted. Practicing in a group can further expand attention and perception because different people often notice different things. Learning what others notice brings new things to our attention and helps us appreciate why reasonable people can see the same situation differently.

Once these skills are introduced, it becomes natural to apply it beyond artwork. What changes when we attend not only to someone’s argument but also to their tone and body language? What changes when we pay attention not only to our thoughts but also to what our bodies are communicating?

Better Decisions Begin Before the Decision-Making

Strategy and leadership courses devote considerable time to decision-making frameworks. We teach people to weigh alternatives, calculate risks, evaluate consequences, and compare costs and benefits. These are important tools to achieve what you want.

Yet, before we even begin choosing among alternatives, we may have unknowingly constrained our options by directing our attention to some things and overlooking others. Decision researchers call this problem “bounded awareness.”

Limited options happen because we cannot evaluate information we fail to see. We cannot question assumptions we do not realize we have. We cannot consider another person’s perspective if we don’t pay attention to what they are communicating. We cannot account for how our emotions affect us if we do not recognize that they are there.

We cannot notice everything, nor should we try. The goal is to become better at directing and widening our attention, because the more we notice, the more choices we have.

item.title: Why We Will Always Love You, Dolly
item.description:
Relationships

Why We Will Always Love You, Dolly

Dolly put love first, beyond divisions. Science explains why we loved her back.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Our love of Dolly Parton transcended divides because her love of others transcended divisions.
  • Dolly knew what mattered most in life, and research supports that she was right.
  • Healthy relationships are the key to health and happiness. The good life is loving others.

Most Americans, and countless millions around the world, are mourning the death of country music legend and philanthropist Dolly Parton, who died Aug. 25 at the age of 80. The tributes and the outpouring of love and grief are testament to the life she lived. In our divided states of America, we are united in our grief. We all feel like we lost a truly great human being. We did. The world was a better place with Dolly Parton in it.

To be honest, I'm not even a country music fan. But my sadness runs deep.

Why was Dolly so universally beloved? What was so special about her that our love for her transcends our divides?

Dolly loved her neighbors - all of them. She knew the truth that we're all neighbors in an interconnected world. Her family, announcing her death, said her warmth "made us all feel like family."

We loved Dolly because Dolly loved everyone.

Rich in Kindness and Love and Understanding

Where does love like that come from? Dolly grew up one of 12 children in a tiny house in the Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee. Economically, the Partons had almost nothing. When little Dolly came home crying because schoolkids had mocked The Coat of Many Colors her mother sewed her from rags, her mother told her she never wanted to hear her say they were poor: "We are rich in kindness and love and understanding." Dolly learned early on that love is true wealth.

Ye Shall Know Them By Their Fruits

Dolly was a Christian who let her love do the talking. Jesus said, "Ye shall know them by their fruits." And Dolly had a standing answer for the fine Christians who pressed her to judge one group of people over another:

"I keep saying, 'If you're the fine Christian that you think you are, why are you judging people? That's God's job,'" she told Larry King. "We're not God, we're not judges, we're supposed to love one another."

article continues after advertisement

Dolly refused to put herself in the judge’s seat or to be put on a pedestal for her kindness and compassion. She poked fun at her own wigs and her own flaws before anyone else could. She didn’t engage in judgmental tirades or sermons about righteousness.

That humility is yet another reason why Dolly was beloved by the right and the left alike. She never forgot who she was or where she came from.

Crediting the Talmud with the insight, Anaïs Nin wrote: "We don't see things as they are. We see them as we are." Because Dolly saw the Good in all her neighbors, it was easy for her to love them. And because she loved everyone, everyone loved Dolly. She radiated joy and love.

The Research Says Dolly Was Right

Dolly knew what mattered most in life and lived that truth. And the research says she was right.

The most robust studies of human happiness keep arriving at the same finding. The Harvard Study of Adult Development—the longest-running study of adult life ever conducted, following people for more than 85 years—found that the strongest predictor of our health and happiness is not wealth, fame, or achievement. It is warm relationships. Robert Waldinger, the psychiatrist who directs the study, compresses eight decades of data into one sentence: "Good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Period."

A landmark analysis of more than 300,000 people, led by psychologist Julianne Holt-Lunstad, found that strong social ties predict roughly 50% greater odds of survival. When psychologist Susan Pinker later ranked what actually keeps us alive, close relationships and social integration came out on top—above smoking, drinking, and exercise.

article continues after advertisement

Basically: when we have strong, loving relationships, we thrive. When we don't, we suffer. Which means the teaching at the heart of every major religion and wisdom tradition—love your neighbor as yourself; treat others as you wish to be treated—aren't just moral teachings. They are essential for survival and human flourishing. The Golden Rule is golden for a reason.

Love and joy are the evolutionary payoffs for strong social bonds, because those bonds kept our ancestors alive. Rich relationships = rich life. This reality is golden. Whether we look through the lens of the spirit or the lens of science, both fingers point to the same moon of truth: loving our neighbors as ourselves is the good life.

Science went looking for the secret of the good life and found what Dolly's mama already knew.

Now Look at Your Own Life

But we don’t have to take science’s word for it—or even Dolly’s. We can know the truth of this for ourselves from ourselves.

Take a moment. Close your eyes. Now, what are some of your happiest times in life? Seek the answers within. Don't stress about getting the list exactly right—it might change tomorrow. Just notice what emerges.

What comes to the surface? How many of those moments involved other people? Times with family, friends, holidays, vacations, and adventures? Deep engagement with others in real life?

Notice something? For nearly all of us, our happiest moments are moments of connectedness—moments beyond the walls of the self. Dolly once put it, "Making memories with those you love is what matters most in life." And it echoes a teaching of Jesus that Dolly lived: we must lose our lives to find them. Our happiest times come when we get beyond the self, beyond ego.

Jesus warned, "For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" Dolly gained the whole world—the fame, the fortune, the hundred million records—and never lost her soul. Her remained rooted to her faith and values.

Dolly liked to say, “If your lucky enough to have more than you need, you’re lucky enough to give.” Dolly gave. As but one example she mailed than 200 million free books to children through her Imagination Library. Love mattered more to Dolly than material things. That was the source of her true wealth. Because she was rich in love, she was rich without measure.

article continues after advertisement

Dolly’s mama was right all along.

What Our Love for Dolly Says About Us

Here's where it gets really interesting. Our collective love of Dolly Parton is a shared recognition of the love in her. We loved Dolly because she was loving.

What does that say about us?

That there is Good in us. Because it takes Good to recognize Good. Dolly saw the Good in us all along —and she gave it right back.

Jesus gave his followers a single identifying mark: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." It isn’t by power or financial wealth, but by love. Dolly understood that the Bullseye of Life is love, and she hit the mark.

And here's one last thing you may not know. In 1973, Dolly wrote her most famous song, "I Will Always Love You," as a goodbye. She was leaving Porter Wagoner—the man whose TV show made her a star. It was a painful professional split. He didn't want her to go. So Dolly said goodbye the only way she knew how: with a love song. Her love transcended divides, which was her lesson to us all.

We will always love you, Dolly, because you loved us first. And the fact that we can still say it together is the reminder you left us: there is Good in all of us.
